title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
What is the Agent Coders Clinic?
The Agent Coders Clinic is a hands-on workshop where you’ll learn to use AI coding agents — tools that can read your files, run commands, edit code, and work through multi-step tasks on your behalf. Whether this is your first time using an AI coding tool or you’ve been experimenting on your own, this clinic will give you a practical workflow you can take back to your daily work.

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
What you’ll learn
By the end of this clinic, you will:

Understand what an agentic coding harness is and how it differs from chatbots or autocomplete
Get Claude Code or Antigravity running on the JupyterHub — no AI account or subscription of your own needed
Practice a clear–handoff–notes workflow that keeps your work organized across sessions
Use an agent to plan and edit a real Quarto book, with a plan and handoff notes between sessions
Teach the agent your workflow (task → branch → pull request) and write skills for tasks you repeat

title: Agent Coders Clinic
text:
The environment
Everything runs on a sandboxed JupyterHub. You have a terminal, a file browser, and your choice of coding tool. Nothing connects to private or confidential systems — this is a safe space for learning and experimenting.

Log in to GitHub. The hub uses your GitHub account to let you in.
Open https://nmfs-openscapes.2i2c.cloud/ . You should see the start a server page.
You can accept the default image. Choose the 4 GB size and click Start. It can take a minute or two to start.

title: Setup
section: Once on the hub, run the setup script.
text:
Once on the hub, run the setup script.

In JupyterLab: File → New → Terminal.
Run the workshop setup script in the terminal.

Choose the tool you are using for the clinic:

Claude CodeAntigravity


In a terminal, run:
~/shared/workshop/claude-agent-coders
The first time you run this, it will ask for your key that starts with sk-. You can find your key in ~/shared/workshop/agentcoders-keys.md (i.e. in the shared directory in your home directory).
First start Start in your home directory. cd ~. The first start will ask a few setup questions. Pick a theme. When it asks whether to trust this folder, say no (since you are not in a directory). This first setup is only to get Claude Code installed and your key saved. If Claude Code starts anyway, type /exit to close it.
Second and later start If you have already done a first start (at any point), then navigate to the directory you want to work in (cd directory-name) and then type claude-agent-coders or ~/shared/workshop/claude-agent-coders.


In the terminal, run the team launcher:
~/shared/agent-coders/agy-agent-coders
The launcher checks for the Antigravity CLI (agy), installs it automatically if missing, sets up your terminal PATH, adds auto-approved everyday commands to your settings, and configures safety guards.
On your first run, it will walk you through sign-in:

When prompted with “Select login method”, choose/accept “Continue with Google Cloud”.
Look for the link in the terminal: click “click to authenticate” (or copy and paste the URL into your browser).
Sign in with your Google account, click through the authorization prompts, and copy the authorization code.
Return to the terminal and paste the code.
Note, it is going to say you have no license. That is ok and correct. You are using pay-as-you-go (except NMFS is paying not you).
When prompted for your Google Cloud project code, paste the project code provided to you (from Jira or your organizer).
When prompted with “Accept License”, accept the ‘Agent Platform’.

Once authentication completes and you see the agent prompt, type /exit to close it so you can complete the repository setup steps below.

text:
GitHub Access
Choose how much of your GitHub the agent can reach:

No access If you are not having the agent push to GitHub, then you don’t have to login to GitHub at all.
Token for one repository: the agent can only push to your practice repository.

Token for one repositoryFull access

Go to https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens/new and fill in:

Token name: JupyterHub Claude Code training
Expiration: a few days after the clinic

Permissions → Repository permissions:

Contents: Read and write

Issues: Read and write

Log in to GitHub with the token

gh auth login
Answer the prompts:

Note, logging in for full access (the Full access tab) replaces the token with full access.









Warning



With this option the agent can read, change and delete anything you can on GitHub, including private repositories. But it cannot reach NMFS GitHub Enterprise (SSO protected).



Log in
In a terminal, run:
gh auth login
Answer the prompts:

Where do you use GitHub? GitHub.com
Preferred protocol for Git operations? HTTPS
Authenticate Git with your GitHub credentials? Yes
How would you like to authenticate? Login with a web browser

It prints a one-time code. Copy it, open the link it shows, paste the code, and approve. When the terminal says you are logged in, you are done.

title: Setup
text:
Good to know

Claude CodeAntigravity



Claude Code budget: In a terminal, claude-agent-coders --budget shows what you have spent, your budget, and when your key expires. Spending shows up about a minute after you use Claude.
Switch models: In Claude, use /model, for example /model claude-opus-4-6 for a hard problem. The default is Claude Sonnet 4.6; see Models & Budget.
Full path: In a terminal, if claude-agent-coders is not found, use ~/shared/workshop/claude-agent-coders.
Your settings are preserved: claude-agent-coders preserves your personal configurations.




Always use the team launcher: Start Antigravity in a terminal with agy-agent-coders, not plain agy. Plain agy asks for permission before every single shell command out of the box; agy-agent-coders adds everyday commands to your settings and guards against destructive actions.
Full path: If agy-agent-coders is not found, use ~/shared/agent-coders/agy-agent-coders.
Do not use agy --sandbox on the hub: The hub’s container security does not support container sandboxing and JupyterHub is already a sandbox.
Your settings are preserved: agy-agent-coders preserves your personal settings and existing configurations.

title: Setup
text:
Guardrails
Once you connect GitHub (see GitHub Access), the agent can do on GitHub whatever your login allows. The two launchers protect you in different ways.

Claude CodeAntigravity


claude-agent-coders adds no guard of its own. Claude Code’s permission mode protects you. The current mode is shown below the prompt box, and Shift+Tab switches between modes.

Auto mode: before each action runs, a second model checks it. Routine work runs without asking. Risky actions are blocked, such as force pushes, git reset --hard, deleting files that were already there, downloading and running scripts, and merging a pull request you have not approved. Auto mode does allow pushing to main, so start each task on a branch.
Manual mode: Claude Code asks before every command and every file edit. Read each one before you approve it. Answering “don’t ask again” for a command means it will not ask about that command again.

claude-agent-coders starts in auto mode, on the default model, Claude Sonnet 4.6. Auto mode needs a Sonnet or Opus model; it is not available with Claude Haiku 4.5. If the mode below the prompt box is not auto, switch back with /model claude-sonnet-4-6 and press Shift+Tab until it shows auto.


agy-agent-coders installs a guard that checks every shell command the agent runs. It watches only the agent. You can still run any of these commands yourself in a terminal.
Always blocked:

git reset --hard, git clean -f, and force pushes (--force-with-lease is allowed)
rm -r outside the folder you started the agent in
Pushing to main (or master). The agent works on a branch and opens a pull request instead.
Deleting a GitHub repository. You do that yourself.

Stops and asks you first:

Merging a pull request
Deleting a branch
Closing an issue
Opening a pull request in a repository you do not own

For these, the agent should tell you what it is about to do and ask. Once you say yes, it runs the command again. For merging and closing issues, Antigravity then shows its own approval prompt too.
These match the workflow in this clinic: one branch per task, a pull request, and you decide when it is merged.

title: Setup
text:
If something goes wrong

Claude CodeAntigravity



claude-agent-coders: command not found: Open a new terminal (new terminals load the updated PATH with ~/.local/bin), or run the full path ~/shared/workshop/claude-agent-coders.
“That workshop code is not right”: Check the code and try again.
“That key was not accepted”: Paste the whole key, starting with sk-. If it still fails, ask your organizer.
“A key for … was already issued”: You, or someone using your name, already signed up. Ask your organizer.
“All workshop keys are handed out”, “sign-up is closed” or “has ended”: Ask your organizer.
“not set up yet” or “Could not reach the workshop gateway”: The gateway is not running. Ask your organizer.
A key from an earlier workshop: Run claude-agent-coders --reset, then claude-agent-coders and enter the new code.




agy-agent-coders: command not found: Open a new terminal (new terminals load the updated PATH with ~/.local/bin), or run the full path ~/shared/agent-coders/agy-agent-coders.
“agent-coders guard: …”: The safety guard stopped a command (see Guardrails). For a blocked one, such as git reset --hard or a push to main, tell the agent to use a safe alternative: git stash, a soft reset, or a branch and a pull request. If it says “needs the user to say yes first”, the agent should ask you before trying again.
Commands asking for confirmation: Prompts to approve actions like pip, cp, mv, or rm are expected behavior for commands not on the everyday whitelist. Review the proposed command and approve it if appropriate.
Google Cloud project prompt: Make sure you paste the exact Google Cloud project code provided in your clinic materials or Jira ticket.

title: Models & Budget
text:
When to switch models

Sonnet — your everyday model, and the default. Use it for most tasks.
Opus — reach for it when Sonnet struggles: complex reasoning, large refactors, subtle bugs. Switch back when you’re done.
Haiku — cheaper, for simple, well-defined work. Auto mode is not available with Haiku, so expect Claude Code to ask before actions.
Open models — interesting to try, but they use file-reading and editing tools less reliably than Claude. If one answers without looking at your files, ask it explicitly (e.g., “use the read tool on notes.txt”).

title: Models & Budget
text:
Switching models
Inside Claude Code, type /model followed by a name from the table, for example /model claude-opus-4-6.

title: Models & Budget
text:
Checking your budget
In any terminal on the hub:
claude-agent-coders --budget
It shows what you have spent, your budget, and when your key expires. Spending shows up about a minute after each request.

title: Models & Budget
text:
Making your budget last

Stay on Sonnet for routine tasks; it is the default for a reason.
Switch to Opus only when you need to, then switch back.
Use /clear between tasks — this resets the conversation, which means the agent sends less context with each request and each request costs less.
The gateway caches repeated context for Claude models, so later requests in a session cost less than the first one.







Tip



Running /usage in Claude Code shows what the current session has spent.

title: What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
The idea
You’ve probably used AI chat — you type a question, you get an answer. Maybe you’ve used autocomplete in an editor, where an AI suggests the next few characters as you type.
An agentic coding tool is different. It’s a program — sometimes called an agentic harness — that gives an AI model access to your actual development environment: your files, your terminal, and your git repository. Instead of just answering questions, it can:

title: What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
Read your files to understand your project
Search across your codebase for patterns or definitions
Edit files directly
Run commands in your terminal (with your permission)
Iterate — check its own work, fix mistakes, and keep going

title: What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
The agent loop
When you give an agentic tool a task, it doesn’t just generate text. It runs a loop:

Think about what to do next
Act — read a file, run a command, make an edit
Observe the result
Repeat until the task is done (or it gets stuck and asks you)

This is why they’re called “agentic” — the model is acting on your behalf, making decisions about what tools to use and in what order.

title: What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
Examples of agentic harnesses
There are several tools that work this way. In this clinic you can use any of them through the shared gateway:

Claude Code — Anthropic’s CLI tool, built for Claude
OpenCode — open-source, works with Claude and open models
GitHub Copilot CLI — GitHub’s coding tool
Gemini CLI — Google’s coding tool

They all follow the same basic pattern: you give a prompt, the agent works through it using tools, and you review the result. The commands and interface differ, but the concept is the same.

title: What Is Agentic Coding?
text:
What an agent is not

It’s not magic — agents make mistakes, especially on complex or ambiguous tasks.
It’s not a chatbot — keep interactions focused on tasks, not open-ended conversation.
It doesn’t remember between sessions — that’s why you use handoff notes.
It needs verification — see Checking the Agent’s Work.

title: How to Work with an Agent
text:
The workflow
An agentic tool is not a chatbot. The biggest mistake people make is treating it like one — free-form messages, tangents, and endless conversations that confuse both you and the agent.
The discipline is simple: one task, one session, one handoff.
flowchart TD
    A["🎯 Pick a task"] --> B["🔍 Plan first"]
    B --> C["🔨 Build small"]
    C --> D{"Done or\nswitching?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["📝 Handoff note\nto notes/"]
    E --> F["/clear"]
    F --> A
    D -- "No, keep going" --> C
That’s the whole thing. Let’s walk through each step.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: How to Work with an Agent
text:
Pick a task
Every session starts with a task — something with a clear scope.







Good tasks
Not tasks




“Draft the introduction chapter”
“Help me with my project”


“Figure out why the PDF won’t render”
“Let’s work on stuff”


“Brainstorm what sections this book needs”
“Tell me about Quarto”


“Write tests for the data-loading function”
“Make everything better”



A task can be planning, research, brainstorming, or building. The point is that it has a boundary.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: How to Work with an Agent
text:
Plan first, build small
Two rules that save time and money:
Plan before you build. Start by asking the agent to explore and make a plan. Save the plan to notes/. Then clear and start a fresh session to execute. Exploration context clutters implementation. In Claude Code, plan mode (press Shift+Tab until it shows below the prompt box) keeps the agent from changing files while you plan.
Build small before building big. One chapter, one function, one section at a time. Review it, then continue. Small pieces are easier to check and cheaper to redo.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: How to Work with an Agent
text:
Close the loop
When you’re done with a task — or switching to a different one — or the conversation is just getting long — close it:

Tell the agent: “I am about to clear. Update the handoff note in notes/handoff.md with what we did and what’s next.”
Run /clear (in Claude Code or Antigravity)
Start the next task fresh

In Skills 100 you teach the agent that “I am about to clear” means all of step 1, so you can stop spelling it out.
The handoff note is a short file — what was done, what’s next, any decisions made. Not a transcript, not a code dump. A sticky note for the next session.
You don’t have to finish to close. “Got halfway through X, next step is Y” is a perfectly good handoff. The next session picks it up.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: How to Work with an Agent
text:
Why this matters






WarningLong conversations cost you three ways




Money — every message resends the entire conversation history
Quality — the agent drifts and loses focus as context piles up
Risk — if the session dies, you lose everything since the last handoff

Short, focused tasks with handoff notes between them are cheaper, more reliable, and easier to pick up later — by you or by someone else on your team.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: How to Work with an Agent
text:
What about /resume?
Most tools can resume the previous session. This works for short interruptions — you stepped away for coffee and want to continue the same task.
But for picking up work after a longer gap, or when someone else is taking over, start fresh:

Read notes/handoff.md and continue where we left off.

This gives the agent exactly the context it needs and nothing it doesn’t. And anyone on the team can pick it up — not just the person who started it.
crumbs: 5  How to Work with an Agent

title: Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
Before you start
In this activity you’ll practice the full clear–handoff–notes workflow from Skills 101. You’ll use an AI coding agent to plan and execute edits to a real Quarto book — the same template this documentation is built on.

text:
Make a copy of the practice repository
Do this on GitHub’s website.

Open the NOAA Quarto book template.
Click Use this template → Create a new repository.
Owner: your personal GitHub username, not an organization.
Repository name: my-quarto-book, or any name you like. The steps below use my-quarto-book.
Choose Public and click Create repository.
Make sure to copy all branches (there is a checkbox).



Clone your repository into the JupyterHub.
Open a terminal in the JupyterHub and type this (replace YOUR-USERNAME):
cd ~

You now have ~/my-quarto-book on the JupyterHub.

title: Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
section: Connect to GitHub so you can push changes
text:
Connect to GitHub so you can push changes
You chose how the agent reaches GitHub in Setup.

Token for one repository: your token must include my-quarto-book. If you made the token before this repository existed, open https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens, click your token, and add my-quarto-book under Repository access. Or make a new token for it and log in again with gh auth login.
Full access: nothing more to do.
No access: you can still do this activity. The agent works and commits on the hub; you just cannot push to GitHub.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
section: Start your agent in your repository
text:
Start your agent in your repository






Important



Always start your agent from inside your project folder (cd ~/my-quarto-book first). The folder you start it in is what your agent treats as the project boundary.


Open a new terminal and start your agent:

Claude CodeAntigravity


cd ~/my-quarto-book
claude-agent-coders
This time, say yes to trusting the folder: this is the repository you want the agent to work in.


cd ~/my-quarto-book
agy-agent-coders




Try a first prompt
Type this:

What is this repository? List the main files and what they do.

If the agent reads your files and answers, you are set up.
What to expect while working:

Claude CodeAntigravity


claude-agent-coders starts in auto mode: routine work runs without asking, and a second model blocks risky actions. Auto mode does allow pushing to main, so keep your work on a branch. See Guardrails.


With agy-agent-coders:

Everyday commands run automatically: everyday tasks—inspecting files (ls, cat, grep, etc.), creating directories (mkdir, touch), R, Quarto, Python, and read-only git/GitHub actions run without asking. It also automatically accepts edits to files inside your project repository.
Unlisted commands ask for approval: Anything not on the team’s auto-approved list (copying, moving, or deleting files, pip, or running other software) will prompt for your confirmation before running. This is normal and expected.
Safety guards: Destructive actions like git reset --hard, force pushes (git push --force), git clean -f, recursive deletions (rm -r) outside your project directory, pushing to main, and deleting a repository are blocked. Merging a pull request, deleting a branch, and closing an issue make the agent stop and ask you first.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
Phase 1: Plan the edits
Goal: Have the agent explore the book and help you plan what to change. Save the plan to notes/. Then clear.

What to do
Ask the agent to look at the book and help you come up with a plan for turning it into something of your own — a project page, a lab notebook, workshop notes, whatever you like. For example:

Read the files in this Quarto book and help me plan how to turn it into [a guide for my lab / notes for my project / a workshop site]. What chapters should I add, remove, or rename? What needs to change in _quarto.yml?

Work with the agent to refine the plan. Go back and forth until you’re happy with it.


Save the plan
When the plan feels ready:

Create a notes/ directory and save our plan to notes/plan.md.



Clear
You’ve finished phase 1. The plan is on disk. Tell the agent you’re about to clear:

I’m about to clear this session. Is there anything else we should save to notes/ before I do?

Then clear:
/clear






Tip



Why clear now? The conversation has gotten long — you’ve been exploring files and discussing options. Clearing resets the context so your next requests are cheaper and more focused. The plan in notes/ has everything the agent needs to continue.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
Phase 2: Execute the plan (Draft 1)
Goal: Have the agent read the plan and execute it. Think about how to approach the work. Clear when done, with a handoff note.

Pick up the plan
Start a fresh prompt:

Read notes/plan.md and the current book structure. We’re going to execute this plan to create a first draft.



Think about how to execute
Before diving in, consider: should you ask the agent to do everything at once, or go step by step?
All at once works when:

The plan is clear and specific
Changes are independent (renaming chapters doesn’t depend on writing content)
You trust the agent to make reasonable choices

Step by step works better when:

You want to review as you go
Steps depend on each other (write chapter 1 before chapter 2 references it)
You’re not sure how the agent will interpret something

A reasonable middle ground: ask the agent to do a logical group of changes, review, then continue. For example:

Start by updating _quarto.yml with the new chapter structure from the plan. Don’t write the chapter content yet — just set up the structure.

Then after reviewing:

Now write first drafts of the new chapters.



Do the work
Execute the plan however you chose. Review what the agent produces. Ask it to fix anything that’s off.


Render and check
When the draft is done:

Render the book with quarto render and check for errors. Fix any problems.



Clear with a handoff note
You’ve finished draft 1. Before clearing, have the agent write a handoff:

Write a handoff note to notes/handoff.md. Summarize what we did, what the book looks like now, and what still needs work.

Review the handoff note — does it capture everything the next session would need? Then clear:
/clear
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
Phase 3: Wrap up
Goal: Practice picking up from a handoff note, then leave a final handoff for what’s next.

Resume from the handoff
Start a fresh prompt:

Read the notes in notes/ and tell me where we are with this book.

The agent should be able to orient itself from the handoff note and tell you the current state without you having to re-explain anything.


Leave a final handoff

Update the handoff note in notes/ with what’s left to do and where to find the information needed to finish. This is the end of the clinic session.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent
text:
Discussion
After the activity, think about:

Did clearing and resuming work? Could the agent pick up from the handoff note without losing important context?
How did you break up the work? All at once vs. step by step — what worked better?
What made a good handoff note? What was missing? What was unnecessary?
How would this workflow help in your real work? Think about projects that span multiple days or involve handoffs between people.







Note



The point of this activity isn’t to produce a perfect book — it’s to practice the workflow. A messy first draft with clean handoff notes is a better outcome than a polished book with no notes.
crumbs: 6  Activity: Edit a Quarto Book with an Agent

title: Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work
text:
Your global instructions file
Every time an agent starts a session, it reads an instructions file in the root of your repo: CLAUDE.md for Claude Code, AGENTS.md for Antigravity. This is where you tell the agent about this project — how to build it, what the architecture looks like.
There’s also a global instructions file in your home directory. It applies to every repo you work in. It’s where you define your personal workflow — the phrases you use, what they mean, and what the agent should do when it hears them.
Think of it as training the agent to work the way you work.
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work

title: Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work
section: Set it up with a prompt
text:
Set it up with a prompt
You don’t need to write the file by hand, or even know where it goes. Start your agent and give it this prompt. It works in Claude Code and Antigravity: the agent works out which file it reads.






NoteCopy-paste this prompt into your agent




Create my global instructions file, the one you read in every project, with my workflow preferences. If you are Claude Code, it is $CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/CLAUDE.md when CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR is set, and ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md otherwise. If you are Antigravity, it is ~/.gemini/config/AGENTS.md. Tell me the path you used.
Here is how I work:
“I am starting a new task” means:

Create a GitHub issue for the task
Create a branch for the task
Work on the branch

“Task is done” or “Let’s finish up the task” means:

Commit the work on the task’s branch, push the branch, and open a PR
Tell me what the PR changes and ask me before merging it
Merge the PR once I say yes
Ask me before deleting the branch

Note: this assumes I’m working on my own. For collaborative work, I’ll open the PR and assign a reviewer instead of merging.
“I am about to clear” or “Get ready to clear” means:

Close any loose ends (pending edits, uncommitted changes). Commit on the task’s branch, never on main; if we are on main, ask me what to do
Review memories for outdated information and update them
Update the handoff note, notes/handoff.md
Keep the handoff concise — move detailed info to separate topic files in notes/ if it’s getting long
Ask me what my next task will be when I return and put that in the handoff

“Initialize this repo” means:

Add an open license if one is missing
Add a reuse statement to the repo
Check the README for basic reproducibility (instructions to run, dependencies listed, clear entry point)

Git rules:

Never push to main. Work on a branch and open a PR
Never use destructive git actions: no --force pushes, no git reset --hard, no git clean -f, no deleting branches that haven’t been merged
Always create new commits rather than amending
Ask before any action that could lose work




The agent will create the file for you. Review it, tweak anything you want, and you’re done.
The GitHub steps (issues, pushing, pull requests) need the GitHub access you set up in Setup. With Token for one repository they work only in that repository. With No access, the agent can still make branches and commits on the hub, but the issue, push and PR steps will fail; tell it to skip them.
Over time, add more shortcuts as you develop habits. The file grows with you.






TipExpect it to stop and ask



When you say “Task is done”, the agent opens the PR and then stops to ask before merging and before deleting the branch. That is on purpose: you decide when work goes into main. With Antigravity, the guardrails enforce this even if the instructions are missing, and Antigravity may show its own approval prompt after you say yes.
If you start working without “I am starting a new task”, the agent is on main. Antigravity’s guard will not let it push there; Claude Code’s auto mode will, unless your instructions stop it. Either way, ask the agent to move the work to a new branch.
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work

title: Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work
text:
Global vs. project instructions









Global
Project (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md)




Where
Your home directory; the agent knows the exact place
The root of your repo


Applies to
Every repo
This repo only


Contains
Your personal workflow and conventions
Project-specific build commands, architecture, coding style


Examples
“Starting a new task” means create issue + branch
“Run quarto render to build”


Persists
Tied to the machine
Committed to the repo, travels with it



Both are loaded at session start. The project file adds context specific to the codebase. The global file carries your workflow everywhere.
Because the global file stays on the machine, it is lost if the hub is rebuilt. If you like what you set up, ask the agent where it is and keep a copy.
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work

title: Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work
text:
Customize it
The prompt above is a starting point. Here are some things you might add over time:

Code style preferences — “Use snake_case for Python, camelCase for JavaScript”
Commit message format — “Start commit messages with a verb: Add, Fix, Update, Remove”
Language — “I work primarily in R and Python”
Review habits — “Always show me a diff summary before committing”

Start simple. Add more when you find yourself repeating the same instruction across sessions.
crumbs: 7  Agent Skills 100: Telling the Agent How You Work

title: Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
The problem
AI coding agents don’t remember anything between sessions. When you start a new session — or run /clear — the agent has no idea what you were doing five minutes ago. It starts fresh every time.
You might think the solution is to build up a huge memory file that the agent loads at the start of every session. But that creates its own problems: the file gets long, stale, and full of context the agent doesn’t need for the current task. It wastes budget re-reading old information.
There’s a simpler approach.
crumbs: 8  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
The workflow: clear, handoff, notes
The core habit is three steps:

1. Work on a task
Start your agent and give it something to do. As it works, it builds up conversation context — the files it has read, the decisions it has made, the changes it has written.


2. Before you stop: handoff
When you’re done with a task (or switching to something else), tell the agent:

I am about to clear.

If you set up your instructions in Skills 100, that phrase is enough: the agent commits loose ends and updates notes/handoff.md. Without it, spell it out:

Update the handoff note in notes/handoff.md with what we did, what’s left, and any decisions we made.

There is one handoff file, and the agent rewrites it each time, so it always describes where things stand now. Git keeps the old versions.


3. Clear and continue
Run /clear (it works in both Claude Code and Antigravity), or close the session. The conversation context is gone, but the handoff note is on disk.
Next time, start the agent and say:

Read the notes in notes/ and pick up where we left off.

The agent reads the handoff, gets oriented, and continues the work.
crumbs: 8  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
section: What goes in a handoff note
text:
What goes in a handoff note
Good handoff notes are short and specific:

What was done (in a sentence or two)
What’s next (the immediate next step)
Any decisions made that aren’t obvious from the code
Blockers or open questions
crumbs: 8  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
section: What does NOT go in a handoff note
text:
What does NOT go in a handoff note

Long detail on one topic — put that in its own file in notes/ and point to it from the handoff
Entire file contents — the agent can read files itself
Code dumps — the code is in the repo
Full project history — keep it to what’s relevant right now
Anything the agent can figure out by looking at the repo







Tip



Think of a handoff note like a sticky note for a colleague: “I finished X, next step is Y, watch out for Z.”
crumbs: 8  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
Example
Here’s what a handoff note might look like:
# Handoff

Updated 2026-09-29.

## Done
- Set up Quarto book structure for clinic docs
- Wrote first drafts of setup and models chapters

## Next
- Write the "What Is Agentic Coding?" chapter
- Check the setup chapter against the hub's current sign-in steps

## Decisions
- Dropped PDF/docx output for now — HTML only until content stabilizes
- Using parts in _quarto.yml to group chapters into sections
- Why we chose HTML only: see notes/output-formats.md
crumbs: 8  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
Why /clear matters
Every message you send includes the entire conversation so far. As the conversation grows, each request sends more tokens and costs more. Running /clear resets this — your next request is cheap again.
The handoff note means you don’t lose anything important. You trade a long, expensive conversation for a short, focused one with a lightweight file to get the agent back up to speed.
crumbs: 8  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
The notes/ directory
Keep handoff notes and working notes in a notes/ directory in your project. This keeps them separate from your actual project files and easy to find.
Some things that work well in notes/:

The handoff note (handoff.md), kept short
Topic notes the handoff points to (notes/output-formats.md, notes/data-sources.md)
Plans and task lists for ongoing work
Analysis summaries from agent tasks (like the reproducibility analysis)
crumbs: 8  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow
text:
Branches and PRs
Clear–handoff–notes fits inside the branch-and-PR workflow from Skills 100:

“I am starting a new task”: the agent makes an issue and a branch
Do the work. Say “I am about to clear” and /clear as often as you need; the handoff note is committed on the branch, so the next session picks it up
“Task is done”: the agent opens a PR and asks before merging

The branch keeps the changes isolated and reviewable. The handoff note lets you, or someone else, pick up work that spans several sessions.
crumbs: 8  Agent Skills 101: The Clear–Handoff–Notes Workflow

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
What is a skill?
A skill teaches the agent a task you do again and again, so it is done the same way every time. Instead of re-explaining a process in every session, you write it down once and the agent follows it.
Think of it as a recipe card for your agent.
Each skill is a short file called SKILL.md, in its own folder, with two parts:
Claude Code and Antigravity both understand this format, so one skill works in either tool.

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
A name and a one-line description of when to use it.
The steps to follow.

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
How it works
At the start of every session, the agent reads only the name and description of each skill it has. It reads the steps only when it needs them. That keeps skills cheap: you can have many without filling up the conversation.
The agent uses a skill in two ways:

You ask for it by name. “Use the render-check skill.” In Claude Code you can also type /render-check.
The agent picks it on its own when your request matches the description. That is why a good description says when to use the skill, not only what it does.

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
What a skill looks like
---
name: render-check
description: Render the Quarto book and fix any errors. Use after editing chapters or _quarto.yml, or when asked to check that the book builds.
---

1. Run `quarto render` in the project root
2. Check the output for errors or warnings
3. If there are errors, read the error message and fix the issue
4. Re-render until it builds cleanly
5. Report what you fixed (if anything)
The part between the --- lines is the name and description. Everything below is the steps.

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
Make one with a prompt
As with your instructions file in Skills 100, you do not need to know where skills go. Ask the agent:






NoteCopy-paste this prompt into your agent




Create a skill for this project named render-check, in the folder where you load skills for this project, so it is committed with the repo. Tell me the path you used.
Description: Render the Quarto book and fix any errors. Use after editing chapters or _quarto.yml, or when asked to check that the book builds.
Steps:

Run quarto render in the project root
Check the output for errors or warnings
If there are errors, read the error message and fix the issue
Re-render until it builds cleanly
Report what you fixed (if anything)




Skills are loaded when a session starts, so /clear or restart the agent before you try it:

Use the render-check skill.

Change the name, description and steps for your own task. You can also ask the agent to turn something you just did together into a skill: “Make a skill from the steps we just followed to clean up the bibliography.”

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
More examples

format-bib
---
name: format-bib
description: Clean up the bibliography file. Use when asked to tidy, check or sort references.bib.
---

1. Read `content/references.bib`
2. Check each entry for:
   - Missing fields (author, title, year, journal/publisher)
   - Inconsistent formatting (e.g., mixed use of curly braces)
   - Duplicate entries (same DOI or matching author+title+year)
3. Fix any issues found
4. Sort entries alphabetically by citation key


new-chapter
---
name: new-chapter
description: Add a new chapter to the Quarto book. Use when asked to add, create or start a chapter.
---

1. Ask me for the chapter title and which part of the book it belongs in
2. Create `content/<short-name>.qmd` with a `title:` in its front matter
3. Add it to `book.chapters` in `_quarto.yml`, in the right part
4. Run `quarto render` and fix any errors
5. Tell me the file name and where it appears in the book

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
Tips for writing skills

Write the description for the agent. Say when to use the skill, with the words you would actually use to ask for it.
Be specific. “Check for problems” is vague. “Run quarto render and check for errors” is actionable.
Use numbered steps. The agent follows them in order.
Include the actual commands. Don’t make the agent guess what to run.
Keep them short. A skill that’s a full page long is probably two skills.

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
Project skills and personal skills
Like instructions, skills can belong to one project or to you:

Project skills are committed with the repo. Anyone who clones it, and any agent working in it, gets them. Good for tasks tied to that project, like render-check.
Personal skills live in your home directory and work in every project. Good for your own habits. Ask the agent for “a personal skill” instead of “a skill for this project”.

title: Agent Skills 102: Skills
text:
Skills vs. instructions









Instructions (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md)
Skills




Purpose
Context and conventions
Reusable task recipes


When it’s read
All of it, at every session start
Name and description at start; steps only when used


Contents
Build commands, architecture, your workflow phrases
Step-by-step procedures



Instructions give the agent background it always needs. Skills give it procedures to follow on demand. If your instructions file is getting long with step-by-step procedures, move them into skills.

title: Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
text:
The problem with “just review it”
Every guide to AI coding tools says “always review what the agent produces.” That’s true, but it’s not very helpful advice — especially when the agent is writing code you couldn’t have written yourself, or making changes across many files at once.
If you’re a scientist learning to code with an agent, the agent may genuinely be a better coder than you are. So how do you verify work you don’t fully understand?
crumbs: 10  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
section: You don’t have to understand every line
text:
You don’t have to understand every line
Verification isn’t about reading every line of code and confirming it’s correct. It’s about checking that the thing works the way you expect it to. You’re the domain expert — you know what the output should look like, what the data means, and what would be wrong.
Good verification questions:

Does it run without errors?
Does the output look right to me — someone who knows this data / this domain?
Did it change anything I didn’t ask it to change?
Can I explain what this does (even if I couldn’t have written it)?
crumbs: 10  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
section: Let the agent break things for you
text:
Let the agent break things for you
Here’s the key insight: you don’t have to be the one who finds the bugs. You can get the agent to stress-test its own work — if you give it the right information.

Give it real data
The agent probably wrote the code using example data or assumptions about your data. Give it the real thing:

Here’s our actual dataset: data/survey-2024.csv. Run the analysis on this and show me the output. Does anything look wrong?

Real data has edge cases — missing values, unexpected formats, outliers — that break fragile code.


Tell it what you know
You’re the domain expert. You know things the agent doesn’t — what reasonable values look like, what relationships should exist in the data, what the previous version produced. Feed that knowledge in:

The count column should never be negative. Are there any negative values in the output?


Last year’s report had 342 sites. If we’re getting a very different number, something is probably wrong.


This function is supposed to handle both CSV and Excel files. Try it with data/samples.xlsx — does it work?



Ask it to write tests
You don’t have to write the tests yourself. But you can tell the agent what to test for:

Write tests that check:

The function handles empty input without crashing
Missing values in the date column don’t cause errors
The output has the same number of rows as the input
Column names match what downstream code expects


You’re providing the domain knowledge about what should be true. The agent provides the testing mechanics.


Ask it to try to break it
This is one of the most useful things you can do:

Try to break this. What inputs would cause it to fail? What assumptions is it making that might not hold?

Agents are good at this — they can reason about edge cases and generate adversarial inputs. Breaking things is good. Every failure reveals something that needs to be more robust.
crumbs: 10  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
text:
A verification workflow
A practical approach:

Does it run? Ask the agent to execute it. Fix any errors.
Does it look right? Review the output with your domain knowledge. Flag anything suspicious.
Feed it real data. Swap in your actual files and see what happens.
Ask it to break it. Have the agent find its own bugs.
Check the diff. Look at what files changed. The pull request from “Task is done” (Skills 100) shows every change on its Files changed tab. Anything unexpected?







Tip



Verification works best as a separate task. After the agent builds something, clear the session, then start a new session focused entirely on testing and breaking what was built. A fresh session means the agent isn’t biased by the decisions it made during implementation.
crumbs: 10  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent’s Work
section: This is a skill you build over time
text:
This is a skill you build over time
Nobody gets this right immediately. The more you work with agents, the better you get at:

Knowing what questions to ask
Spotting when output “looks off”
Giving the agent the right information to test against

For now, the most important habit is: don’t just accept what the agent produces. Run it, look at it, and throw some real data at it before you call it done.
crumbs: 10  Agent Skills 103: Checking the Agent's Work

title: Tool Comparison
text:
Quick reference
On the JupyterHub, the clinic provides pre-configured launchers for Claude Code (via the clinic’s LiteLLM Bedrock gateway) and Antigravity (via Google Cloud). Other tools remain available for reference if running in your own environment.

Claude Code

title: Tool Comparison
text:
Key differences
Claude Code connects to the clinic’s LiteLLM gateway on Amazon Bedrock. It has built-in commands for managing context (/clear), checking status and spending (/status, /usage, claude-agent-coders --budget), and switching models (/model). It reads CLAUDE.md or @AGENTS.md in the project root.
Antigravity (agy) is Google’s agentic coding CLI powered by Gemini models. On the hub, the agy-agent-coders launcher installs agy, pre-approves everyday tasks (Quarto, R, Python, git, file inspections) so they run without interruption, and sets a safety guard that blocks destructive commands (git reset --hard, force push, rm -r outside project, pushing to main, deleting a repository) and makes the agent ask before merging, deleting branches or closing issues. Claude Code has no launcher guard; its auto mode (Sonnet or Opus only) blocks risky actions, and its manual mode asks before everything. It reads AGENTS.md in the project root.
OpenCode is open-source and has flexible model configuration, connecting to open models through gateways.
GitHub Copilot CLI is focused on command-line suggestions and interactive coding assistance through GitHub Copilot.

title: Tool Comparison
text:
Common commands across tools
Regardless of which tool you use, you’ll do the same basic things:

Give a prompt — type what you want the agent to do
Approve tool use — agents ask permission before running unapproved commands or modifying sensitive files
Review output — always check what the agent did before moving on
End the session or reset — close the tool or clear context (/clear) when switching tasks

title: Using Your Own Google Cloud Project (Vertex)
text:
What you need
In the clinic, the workshop pays for your agent’s model calls. After the clinic, NOAA staff can use the USAI models through Google Cloud Vertex AI, billed to a Google Cloud project. This page shows how to set up Claude Code, OpenCode, Antigravity, or GitHub Copilot CLI on your own Linux, Mac, or Windows computer to use your project.
Which models you get depends on what your project has turned on, not on the tool. If a model is not turned on, the tool will report that the model was “not found”.
The NOAA USAI catalog includes Google’s Gemini models (for example gemini-3.8-flash and gemini-3.1-pro-preview), Anthropic’s Claude models (for example claude-opus-5-5, claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-haiku-5-5), xAI’s Grok models, and OpenAI’s gpt-oss-120b-maas. Each Claude model needs its own approval in your project before you can use it. If you plan to use Claude, ask for approval of the specific models you want, for example claude-sonnet-5-5 and claude-opus-5-5.
crumbs: 12  Using Your Own Google Cloud Project (Vertex)

title: Using Your Own Google Cloud Project (Vertex)
text:
A Google Cloud project with Vertex AI and the models you want turned on. At NOAA this comes through the USAI program. You need the project ID, which looks like my-project-123456 (not the display name).
Permission to install software on your computer. On a NOAA-managed computer, you may need IT to install these tools for you.
crumbs: 12  Using Your Own Google Cloud Project (Vertex)

title: Using Your Own Google Cloud Project (Vertex)
text:
Install your harness
The harness is the program you talk to; the model behind it runs on Google Cloud. Install the one you want to use. On Linux and Mac, run the command in a terminal. On Windows, run it in PowerShell.

Claude CodeOpenCodeAntigravityCopilot CLI


Linux and Mac:
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Windows (PowerShell):
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex
Claude Code on Windows also needs Git for Windows. Other ways to install are in the Claude Code documentation.


Linux and Mac:
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
Windows: run the same command in Git Bash, or see the other ways to install in the OpenCode documentation.


Linux and Mac:
curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash
Windows (PowerShell):
irm https://antigravity.google/cli/install.ps1 | iex
The command it installs is called agy.


Linux and Mac:
curl -fsSL https://gh.io/copilot-install | bash
Windows (PowerShell):
winget install GitHub.Copilot
Other ways to install are in the Copilot CLI documentation. With Vertex you do not need a GitHub Copilot subscription.



Close the terminal and open a new one, so it finds the newly installed command.
crumbs: 12  Using Your Own Google Cloud Project (Vertex)

title: Using Your Own Google Cloud Project (Vertex)
section: Tell your harness to use Vertex
text:
Tell your harness to use Vertex

Claude CodeOpenCodeAntigravityCopilot CLI


1. Sign in to Google Cloud. Claude Code uses your Google login through the Google Cloud CLI (gcloud). Install the Google Cloud CLI, then run this once:
gcloud auth application-default login
A browser opens. Sign in with your NOAA Google account.
2. Set three environment variables. Replace YOUR_PROJECT_ID with your project ID.
Linux and Mac:
export CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1
export CLOUD_ML_REGION=global
export ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID=YOUR_PROJECT_ID
These last only for this terminal. To have them in every new terminal, add the three lines to the end of your shell’s startup file: ~/.zshrc on a Mac, ~/.bashrc on most Linux systems.
Windows (PowerShell):
setx CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX 1
setx CLOUD_ML_REGION global
setx ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID YOUR_PROJECT_ID
setx saves them for every new PowerShell window, but not the one you typed them in. Open a new window before the next step.
3. Start Claude Code:
claude
It should not ask you to log in to an Anthropic account. If it does, the environment variables are not set in this terminal.
Choosing a model. Type /model inside Claude Code, or start it with claude --model claude-opus-5-5. Use the model names your project has turned on.
Region. global lets Google route each request to wherever there is capacity. If your project requires requests to stay in the United States, use us instead of global.


1. Sign in to Google Cloud. OpenCode uses your Google login through the Google Cloud CLI (gcloud). Install the Google Cloud CLI, then run this once:
gcloud auth application-default login
A browser opens. Sign in with your NOAA Google account.
2. Set two environment variables. Replace YOUR_PROJECT_ID with your project ID.
Linux and Mac:
export GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=YOUR_PROJECT_ID
export VERTEX_LOCATION=global
These last only for this terminal. To have them in every new terminal, add the two lines to the end of your shell’s startup file: ~/.zshrc on a Mac, ~/.bashrc on most Linux systems.
Windows (PowerShell):
setx GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT YOUR_PROJECT_ID
setx VERTEX_LOCATION global
setx saves them for every new PowerShell window, but not the one you typed them in. Open a new window before going on.
3. List the Claude models your project has. OpenCode’s built-in model list adds a suffix (@default) to newer Claude model names, and Vertex rejects it with a “not found” error. Create a file called opencode.json in OpenCode’s settings folder (~/.config/opencode/ on Linux and Mac, %USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode\ on Windows) with the models your project has turned on, for example:
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "provider": {
    "google-vertex-anthropic": {
      "models": {
        "claude-opus-5-5": { "name": "Claude Opus 5.5" }
      }
    }
  }
}
4. Start OpenCode with one of those models:
opencode -m google-vertex-anthropic/claude-opus-5-5


Antigravity does not use environment variables or gcloud for this. You give it your project when you sign in. Start it:
agy

When asked to “Select login method”, choose “Continue with Google Cloud”.
A browser opens (or the terminal shows a link to open). Sign in with your NOAA Google account and allow access. If the terminal asks for a code, copy it from the browser and paste it in.
It may say you have no license. That is expected: your project pays as you go.
When asked for your Google Cloud project, enter your project ID.
When asked to accept a license, accept “Agent Platform”.

To switch to a different project later, type /logout inside Antigravity, start it again, and sign in with the other project ID.


Copilot CLI can use the Gemini and gpt-oss models in your project, but not Claude. It talks to Vertex through Vertex’s OpenAI-style connection, and Vertex does not offer Claude that way. For Claude, use Claude Code or OpenCode.
1. Sign in to Google Cloud. Copilot CLI uses your Google login through the Google Cloud CLI (gcloud). Install the Google Cloud CLI, then run this once:
gcloud auth application-default login
A browser opens. Sign in with your NOAA Google account.
2. Set four environment variables. Replace YOUR_PROJECT_ID with your project ID. The third one tells Copilot CLI to ask gcloud for a fresh sign-in token for each request; Google’s tokens expire after an hour, so a token pasted in once would stop working.
Linux and Mac:
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_TYPE=openai
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL="https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/locations/global/endpoints/openapi"
export COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY_COMMAND="gcloud auth application-default print-access-token"
export COPILOT_MODEL=google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview
These last only for this terminal. To have them in every new terminal, add the four lines to the end of your shell’s startup file: ~/.zshrc on a Mac, ~/.bashrc on most Linux systems.
Windows (PowerShell):
setx COPILOT_PROVIDER_TYPE openai
setx COPILOT_PROVIDER_BASE_URL "https://aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/YOUR_PROJECT_ID/locations/global/endpoints/openapi"
setx COPILOT_PROVIDER_API_KEY_COMMAND "gcloud auth application-default print-access-token"
setx COPILOT_MODEL google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview
setx saves them for every new PowerShell window, but not the one you typed them in. Open a new window before going on.
3. Start Copilot CLI:
copilot
It should not ask you to log in to GitHub. If it does, the environment variables are not set in this terminal.
Choosing a model. Change COPILOT_MODEL and start Copilot CLI again. Model names start with who makes them: google/gemini-3.8-flash (faster and cheaper), google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview, or openai/gpt-oss-120b-maas.

title: Using Your Own Google Cloud Project (Vertex)
text:
Check that it works
Ask the agent something short, like “reply with just the word hi”. If it answers, your project is working.







What you see
What it usually means




“not found” or “does not have access” for a model
That model is not turned on in your project, or the region does not have it. For Claude, each model needs its own approval. Try another model, or ask your project’s administrator.


Copilot CLI says a Claude model is “not servable”
Copilot CLI cannot use Claude on Vertex. Use a Gemini model, or use Claude Code or OpenCode for Claude.


“could not load the default credentials” or another credentials message
Run gcloud auth application-default login again (Claude Code, OpenCode and Copilot CLI).


Claude Code asks you to log in to Anthropic, or Copilot CLI to GitHub
The environment variables are not set in this terminal. On Windows, open a new PowerShell window after setx.


Permission denied on the project
Your Google account is not a member of the project, or not allowed to use Vertex AI in it. Ask your project’s administrator.


The command is not found right after installing
Open a new terminal so it picks up the new install.

text: Setup problems

title: Troubleshooting
text:
claude-agent-coders: command not found or agy-agent-coders: command not found
The short command names work only in terminals opened after you first ran the launcher script (the scripts add ~/.local/bin to your PATH). Open a new terminal, or use the full paths:

Claude Code: ~/shared/workshop/claude-agent-coders
Antigravity: ~/shared/agent-coders/agy-agent-coders



“agent-coders guard: …”
The safety guard installed by agy-agent-coders stopped a command. See Guardrails for the full list.

Blocked (git reset --hard, git push --force without lease, git clean -f, rm -r outside your project, pushing to main, deleting a repository): this is intentional. Tell the agent to use a safe alternative, such as git stash, a soft reset, or a branch and a pull request. If you really want one of these, run it yourself in a terminal.
“needs the user to say yes first” (merging a pull request, deleting a branch, closing an issue, a pull request into someone else’s repository): the agent should tell you what it wants to do and ask. If you agree, say so, and it will run the command again.



Antigravity prompts for approval on everyday commands
If Antigravity prompts you to approve simple commands like ls or quarto, you may have started plain agy instead of the team launcher. Quit and restart with:
agy-agent-coders
You can check what commands are currently allowed to run without asking by running:
agy-agent-coders --check


Antigravity prompts for approval on pip, cp, or rm
This is normal and expected. The team launcher whitelists safe, everyday commands (quarto, R, python3, git, directory listing, etc.), but intentionally leaves package installations (pip), file copies, and deletions to require explicit user approval. Review the proposed command and approve it if appropriate.


“That workshop code is not right”
Check the code with your organizer and try again.


“That key was not accepted”
Paste the whole key, starting with sk-. If it still fails, ask your organizer.


“A key for … was already issued”
You, or someone using your name, already signed up. Ask your organizer.


“All workshop keys are handed out”, “sign-up is closed” or “has ended”
Ask your organizer.


“not set up yet” or “Could not reach the workshop gateway”
The gateway is not running. Ask your organizer.


I have a key from an earlier workshop
Forget the old key, then start again and enter the new code:
claude-agent-coders --reset
claude-agent-coders


GitHub refuses a push or gh command

Token for one repositoryFull access


Check these before widening the token:

Are you logged in with the token? Run gh auth status. If you are not logged in, or it shows a browser login, run gh auth login again and choose Paste an authentication token.
Is the remote HTTPS? Run git remote -v. If it starts with git@github.com:, switch it: git remote set-url origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/my-quarto-book.git.
Is this repository on the token? At https://github.com/settings/personal-access-tokens, open the token and check that the repository is in its selected repositories, and that Contents (and Pull requests or Issues, if that is what failed) are Read and write.
Has the token expired? Make a new one with the same settings and log in with it again.

gh repo create does not work with this token, because it cannot create repositories. Create new repositories on GitHub’s website.


Run gh auth status to see whether you are logged in. If not, run gh auth login again and choose GitHub.com, HTTPS, Yes (authenticate Git), and Login with a web browser. If gh repo create says the name already exists, pick a different repository name.





Sandbox fails with agy --sandbox
Do not use --sandbox. The JupyterHub container environment does not support nested container namespaces.


Non-interactive agy -p exits early
agy -p "..." stops immediately at the first command that requires confirmation. For clinic exercises, use interactive mode (agy-agent-coders) instead.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Budget problems

“Budget exceeded”
Your key has hit its spending limit. Ask the organizer — they can increase it or issue a new key.


“Key expired” or “Key blocked”
The key’s time limit is up, or it was switched off. Ask the organizer for a new one.


How to check your remaining budget
claude-agent-coders --budget
Spending shows up about a minute after each request.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Agent behavior problems

Agent gives generic answers without reading files
Some models (especially open models) don’t use file-reading tools reliably. Try:

Being explicit: “Use the read tool to look at README.md, then answer.”
Switching to a Claude model, which handles tool use more reliably.



Agent seems confused or stuck
The conversation may have gotten too long. Run /clear and start fresh. If you have handoff notes in notes/, tell the agent to read those for context.


Agent makes changes you didn’t ask for
Review what the agent is doing before approving. Most tools ask permission before writing files. If it’s going off track, interrupt it and clarify what you actually want.


Agent is working in the wrong folder
Agents work in the folder you start them from. For Antigravity, this folder also defines the boundary that the safety guard protects. Quit (/exit), cd into your repository, and launch the agent again.
